transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. _____. What brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Well, it’s a bit of a long story, but I guess I’m here because work has just become... well, it’s always been demanding, but lately it’s just incredibly frustrating to get through the day. I’m a medical services manager, you see, so I oversee a lot of the administrative side of things for our clinics. I’ve been doing this for years, I have my degree, I know how the system works inside and out, and I usually take a lot of pride in being on top of things. But recently, the day-to-day tasks are just... they feel impossible. 

I mean, I’ll sit down at my desk, and I tell myself, "Okay, we are going to focus right now." I have my coffee, my door is closed, everything is set up perfectly to just get the work done. But what finally pushed me to actually make this appointment and come in today is that I can start pulling an EPIC quality report—which is something I do all the time, it's standard—or I'll sit down in one of our weekly clinic metrics meetings with every intention of tracking the data, and then... I don't even know where my brain goes. 

Within just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far away from what I'm supposed to be doing. I'll catch myself just staring at my monitor, literally rereading the exact same row of numbers over and over again without absorbing a single thing. Or I'll be in that metrics meeting, nodding along, looking right at the person presenting, and suddenly I realize I have completely missed the whole point of the discussion. And it’s embarrassing, frankly. I’ll have to try to piece it together from context clues, which isn’t great when you’re the one supposed to be managing the workflow. It’s like my brain just unplugs itself right when I need it to be locked in, and no matter how hard I try to force myself to just pay attention to the report or the speaker, I just drift off into my own thoughts. So, I just really needed to talk to someone about it, because I can't keep functioning like this.
Did these attention and distractibility problems also happen when you were a child or teenager?

You know, it’s funny you ask that, because I was actually just thinking about this the other day. I was going through some old boxes in the attic—you know how it is when you get on a kick trying to declutter the house on a weekend—and I happened to find a folder with a bunch of my old report cards from elementary school. And it really struck me, because almost every single one of them had the exact same kind of comment in the little notes section at the bottom. The teachers would always write that I was a very bright girl, but that I was just so careless. "Bright but careless," year after year. 

And seeing that really took me back, because I vividly remember what evenings were like at my house growing up. My poor mother, she was an absolute saint, she would literally have to pull up a chair and sit right next to me at the kitchen table every single night just to make sure I actually finished my homework. If she got up to stir a pot on the stove or go answer the telephone, I'd just be off in my own world, staring at the wallpaper pattern or playing with my eraser. 

And honestly, half the time, even getting to the homework stage was a whole ordeal in itself because I was constantly losing track of my assignments. I'd be handed a worksheet, and then it would just vanish into the abyss of my desk at school, or I'd get all the way home—we lived about four blocks from the school, so I usually walked—and I'd open my backpack at that kitchen table and realize I had completely forgotten the spelling workbook or the math book I needed to actually do the work. I can't tell you how many times my mom had to sigh, put her coat back on, and walk with me back to the school to see if the janitor would let us into my classroom to get my books. 

So, yes, I suppose this isn't entirely a new thing at all. It's just... well, it's always been there, just playing out differently when I was younger, I guess. I always just thought I was a bit of a daydreamer or just naturally disorganized, you know? But looking back, it really was a daily struggle for my parents just to keep me on track with the most basic schoolwork, much like how I'm struggling to keep myself on track with these clinic reports now.
Do you also tend to feel physically restless, like you have trouble sitting still?

No, not really. I mean, I know what you mean—my nephew, my sister's boy, he's like that. He literally cannot sit in a chair without bouncing his leg or getting up to pace around the room, but I’ve never really had that problem. 

Actually, I’m quite the opposite, I think. I can sit at my desk for hours. In fact, that’s almost part of the problem, because I’ll sit there, perfectly still, staring at my computer screen with the EPIC system open, and my body is completely stationary, but my mind is just... gone. It’s a million miles away. I don't feel that urge to get up and run around or tap my fingers or anything like that. I’m perfectly comfortable just sitting in my office chair. I have a very nice ergonomic chair, actually, which helps, because I do spend so much time just sitting there trying to force myself to work. 

But no, I don't feel physically restless at all. It's more of an internal thing, you know? The restlessness is all in my head, just jumping from one thought to another, but outwardly, I'm just sitting there like a statue. So, no, I wouldn't say I have any trouble sitting still. If anything, I sit too still while my brain does all the wandering.
